positions.commentary: The speaker states they are open to investing in NVIDIA but notes that insiders cannot predict its future revenues and cash flows five or ten years out.
The speaker notes that technology businesses generally have high returns on equity and are a good place to be as long as one is not paying too much.
The speaker observes that on the day the NASDAQ peaked, Berkshire hit a multi-year low, noting that people were selling Berkshire to buy dot-com companies.
The speaker mentions that if one only wants to buy things at a trailing P.E. of 0.1, one would find those companies, implying such opportunities exist.

thesis: The episode argues that investors should focus on buying quality technology businesses with high returns on equity at reasonable prices, rather than trying to predict long-term revenue growth. It highlights that specific deep-value opportunities, such as buying at one-third of book value or a trailing P.E. of 0.1, do exist for those willing to look, while noting that insiders cannot accurately forecast future cash flows for high-growth firms like NVIDIA.

claims.claim: The speaker states they are open to investing in NVIDIA but notes that insiders cannot predict its future revenues and cash flows five or ten years out.
claims.quote: I mean, the insiders of NVIDIA couldn't tell us what it looks like five or ten years from now in terms of revenues and cash flows. They might have some difficulties with that. So people on the outside looking in would have even greater difficulties.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions that if one only wants to buy things at one-third of book value, one would find those companies, implying such opportunities exist.
claims.quote: And if you said, I only want to buy things at one-third of book value, you would find those as well. So you can set any criteria you want and Mr. Market will give you give you companies that fit that criteria.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that technology businesses generally have high returns on equity and are a good place to be as long as one is not paying too much.
claims.quote: And technology basically has the nuance of having high returns on equity for the most part. And it's a good place to be. So as long as you're not paying too much, you know, it's always great to be in businesses that have growth and that have high returns on equity.

claims.claim: The speaker observes that on the day the NASDAQ peaked, Berkshire hit a multi-year low, noting that people were selling Berkshire to buy dot-com companies.
claims.quote: The day the NASDAQA peaked, I think March 9, 2000, was the day Berkshire hit a multi-year low. So people were literally selling Berkshire to buy Pets.com and Chemdex.com and whatever else was happening then.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions that if one only wants to buy things at a trailing P.E. of 0.1, one would find those companies, implying such opportunities exist.
claims.quote: You would find those. If you said that I only want to buy things at a trailing P.E.E. of 0.1, you would find those too. And if you said, I only want to buy things at one-third of book value, you would find those as well.

numbers.what: the growth of the speaker's personal investment portfolio from 1994 to 2000
numbers.quote: I had a million dollars for the first time I had cash in the bank. And about five years later, the million was about 13 million.

numbers.what: the performance of Pabrai Funds from 1999 to 2007 before fees
numbers.quote: And Pabri Funds, I think from 99 to like 2007, we did, before fees, we did 37% a year.

numbers.what: the percentage of the portfolio that was tech from 1994 to 1999/2000
numbers.quote: Almost the entire portfolio was tech at that time, probably 80, 90% was tech.

numbers.what: the amount lost by the speaker on a failed dot-com business
numbers.quote: I had privately started a dot com and it failed. And that was painful. I mean, I lost about $3 million.

numbers.what: the amount lost by outside investors on the speaker's failed dot-com business
numbers.quote: I had some outside investors that lost about $2 million.

numbers.what: the duration of no down years for Pabrai Funds
numbers.quote: And Pabri Funds, I think from 99 to like 2007, we did, before fees, we did 37% a year. No down years for about eight years.
